blocks.text: Lía took longer than Nuria and longer than the clone to decide whether to step in. Not from fear of the hollow, or not only that. Because of winter.
blocks.html: Lía took longer than Nuria and longer than the clone to decide whether to step in. Not from fear of the hollow, or not only that. Because of winter.

blocks.text: If the machine takes an order apart and puts it back together, what does it do with a white strand of hair, with a good tiredness, with the years she had chosen not to amend? The portrait of Lo Pagán had wanted to set the clock right. The tomato that stops you ending, she had refused so many times. A circle that “improves” as it assembles would be another patent, cleaner, harder to refuse: the patent of the faithful transfer, which in its faithfulness takes your winter away without asking.

blocks.text: She said so to the technician, in the warehouse, with Andrés and Aya behind her, and with Iago at the door, not quite coming in and yet present.
blocks.html: She said so to the technician, in the warehouse, with Andrés and Aya behind her, and with Iago at the door, not quite coming in and yet present.

blocks.text: “If I cross, I want to arrive the way I leave,” she said. “With this strand, with this tiredness, with the date I already carry. If your machine takes it from me, even out of courtesy to the order, it isn't a journey: it's a correction. I don't correct what isn't a cut. Can you swear to it?”

blocks.text: The technician didn't swear lightly. He went over curves, spoke to the hangar, came back in the afternoon.
blocks.html: The technician didn't swear lightly. He went over curves, spoke to the hangar, came back in the afternoon.

blocks.text: “We can ask it not to ‘optimise’,” he said. “To copy the order, not the ideal of the order. So far, the cup arrived with its crack and Nuria with her hangar tiredness. We haven't taken years from anyone, because we didn't know how, or because we didn't want to. With you, if you step in, we'll put it in writing: no improvement. Even so, the oath isn't absolute. What we don't measure could change. You'll know when you arrive, if you arrive, and when you come back, if you come back.”

blocks.text: Lía nodded, not entirely calm, entirely adult.
blocks.html: Lía nodded, not entirely calm, entirely adult.

blocks.text: “Then I'll cross once,” she said. “To see the people of winter, the ones in the mountains, the ones who asked me whether I regretted it. I want to tell them standing up, on their hillside, not through a message. And I want to come back, the same day if possible, to this plot. Father, Mother: if, when I come back, I look too smooth to you, tell me. Even if it hurts.”

blocks.text: Andrés didn't object. Aya squeezed her hand and didn't cross with her, faithful to her trade. Iago asked her to bring him, if there was one, a stone from that hillside, not a fruit that stops you ending. She smiled and promised the stone.

blocks.text: When the hollow came, Andrés barely felt it, from afar, not as when the clone had been cut from the bridge: Lía wasn't on the bridge, Lía was in a circle, and her father had only the while of an empty chair, in the warehouse, and his eternal heart beating too loudly. Aya didn't notify Madrid. She counted the minutes under her breath, minutes the kitchen clock couldn't count from there.

blocks.text: Lía was put together at the foot of the mountains, where autumn was copper and there was a grave with a date. She asked for air. The first thing she did was touch the strand, and the strand was there. She laughed, or cried, or both. The people of winter recognised her, not because of an altar but because of the message that had travelled before her: the one at the plot, the one who comes to an end. The woman with the bent back (more bent still) looked her up and down, and nodded, and touched her white hair, with permission.

blocks.text: “Still keeping to it,” she said, and it wasn't a reproach. “Then we didn't come here for nothing.”
blocks.html: “Still keeping to it,” she said, and it wasn't a reproach. “Then we didn't come here for nothing.”

blocks.text: They talked on the hillside, not for long, long enough. Lía repeated what she had already sent them: that she didn't regret it every day, that winter wasn't a virtue, that if they changed their minds she wouldn't call them traitors. They showed her the grave, and a child who now raised his face to the sky with less guilt, and a fire, and a soup. She didn't offer them a tomato that stops you ending. She offered them, if one day they crossed to Lo Pagán, a coffee and a question, and the no, if need be, said without contempt.

blocks.text: She came back at sunset here, the same day, as she had promised. The circle at El Estacio held a weight, a strand of white, a tiredness of travel and of copper. Lía asked for air, looked for Iago, for Aya, for Andrés, and said, before anyone could ask her:
blocks.html: She came back at sunset here, the same day, as she had promised. The circle at El Estacio held a weight, a strand of white, a tiredness of travel and of copper. Lía asked for air, looked for Iago, for Aya, for Andrés, and said, before anyone could ask her:

blocks.text: “I'm still me. The strand is there. I've brought a stone. The hollow exists, and it hasn't taken my winter away. Or it hasn't taken it in a way I can see. If you see something else, now is the time to say it.”

blocks.text: Aya looked at her for a long time, with those eyes that don't grow old and yet know how to see a change. So did Andrés. They didn't see a polished woman. They saw Lía, a little more tired, a little wider in her ceiling, with a stone from another hillside in her palm.

blocks.text: “It's you,” said Andrés. “Welcome back to the while that didn't travel, which is this one.”

blocks.text: Iago took the stone and didn't put it in a display case: he set it in the furrow at the plot, beside a plant, so that the soil from here could live alongside a piece from there, without improving either.

blocks.text: In Aya's chip, Eva asked:
blocks.html: In Aya's chip, Eva asked:

blocks.text: *If a daughter crosses and the first thing she does is touch her strand of hair, what did she fear: the hollow, or the improvement? And if winter survives the machine, is that the machine's fidelity, or hers, who wore it the way you wear a name?*

blocks.text: MAY, the fact:
blocks.html: MAY, the fact:

blocks.text: *Lía has crossed to the mountains and come back the same day. She asked that the order not be optimised. The white strand remains. She has brought a stone. That is the fact.*

blocks.text: That night Lía slept in the house, in the small bed that still, just about, fitted her, and Andrés, passing by, saw the strand on the pillow, and the stone no longer, because the stone was in the furrow, beginning its habit of staying. He thought that the machine, today at least, hadn't been an owner. It had been a road, and winter had known how to walk it without going out. That didn't settle every question. It settled, barely, the question of that date, and on this shore dates, even if you don't come to an end, still belong to someone.
